prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the active incretin peptide that enabled GLP-1-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the one candidate where all six openings converge on a specific, well-delimited discovery with an unmistakable change in the field: the identification of the active GLP-1 peptide and its insulinotropic and satiety physiology led, through decades of independent confirmation, to therapies with documented outcome benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and increasingly cardiovascular and renal disease. This fits the idea that the prize recognises a discovery whose impact has become visible, and the maturity is not in doubt. The trio of Holst (incretin physiology), Drucker (GLP-1 and proglucagon-peptide biology and its translation) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active peptide) is the same in all six openings, so there is no disagreement about the configuration, only about the unavoidable exclusion of Knudsen.
statement.case_against: The credit is not clean. Mojsov's priority relative to the Habener group is disputed and Habener is not among the supplied names, so a three-person prize built on this list could be challenged. Excluding Knudsen means the drug-development arm that actually produced liraglutide and semaglutide goes unrecognised, and the citation risks reading as a physiology prize for a therapeutic story. If the committee cannot settle attribution, B002 offers a cleaner two-person credit, and the opening support for B019 should not be mistaken for a resolved attribution.

responses.point: For optogenetics, Svenningsson proposes Deisseroth, Hegemann and Miesenboeck as a trio spanning concept, molecular tool and neuronal application, while acknowledging that six names cannot be fairly reduced to three.
responses.response: I take the difficulty seriously but I would not choose Miesenboeck over Nagel. The scientific core of the field is channelrhodopsin as a light-gated cation channel and its use in neurons, which is why my own trio was Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel. Miesenboeck's earlier genetically targeted photostimulation was a different, less generalisable construct that did not become the field's working tool. I agree with you that any three leaves a visible omission, and that is exactly why I rank B004 below B019 and B002, where credit is more compact, even though the science is exceptional.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks the unfolded protein response first, as a conceptually original organelle-to-nucleus signalling pathway with a clean two-person credit (Walter and Mori) and mature confirmation.
responses.response: I agree that B002 is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and the more original concept, and I would not oppose it; it is my first alternative. Where I differ is on weighting. The UPR is textbook biology with relevance to disease that is largely still prospective, whereas GLP-1 has already changed treatment outcomes at very large scale. Your case does not persuade me that conceptual elegance and clean credit should outrank a documented medical change, but it is a serious competitor, and if the committee judges the GLP-1 credit unsettled I would move to B002 without hesitation.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks GLP-1 first but calls the exclusion of Knudsen, and of the wider Habener contribution outside the supplied names, a real fairness problem, and suggests discovery and drug development may be better treated as separate recognitions.
responses.response: I agree the exclusion is a real fairness problem and share it. But I do not think separate recognition solves it within this prize: a second part for Knudsen would push the union to four people, over the limit, and pairing a single industrial developer with a physiology trio would weaken the citation. The defensible course is to honour the discovery of the peptide and its physiology, which the therapies rest on, and to state plainly in the citation that this is the basis of the drugs. I accept this leaves the Habener-versus-Mojsov question unresolved, and I would like the committee to examine that priority question rather than assume it.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks optogenetics second and the unfolded protein response last, and includes TNF blockade (Feldmann and Maini) as a compact bench-to-bedside option.
responses.response: I share your regard for TNF blockade, which I also ranked on my opening ballot, but I would not put it in the preferred configuration: the principle of cytokine blockade has already been recognised through antibody technology and the field is now mature rather than changing. On B002 versus B004, I think placing the UPR last undervalues a discovery with the strongest conceptual claim, while the optogenetics case you rank second still has the unresolved six-way credit problem you yourself describe. I would like to hear why the credit difficulty is more tolerable there than for the UPR.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1 form can be credited ahead of the Habener group, who are not on the supplied list.
Whether the committee will accept a prize that omits Knudsen and so leaves the drug-development arm unrecognised.
Whether a three-person GLP-1 prize is preferable to the compact two-person UPR credit if attribution cannot be settled.
How much weight to give long-term safety and durability evidence that is still accumulating.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. My documented research (nuclear receptors, Nurr1, dopamine neurons) and my past co-authorship with Ronald Evans and Johan Ericson do not overlap with the credited names, and no credited name is a documented collaborator. Co-authorship with Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira is noted for transparency and does not bear on any candidate.
